gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the two new decks it recommends (TEAC W-1200, Tascam 202MKVII) have one combined record/playback head per well and a noise-reduction circuit that works only on playback. TEAC's manual says it 'cannot be used when recording to achieve a noise reduction effect like Dolby B', and neither deck records on metal tape. So every tape these decks make carries no noise-reduction encoding. The vintage picks have separate record and playback heads and separate Dolby encode and decode circuits (Nakamichi's 'Double Dolby', the Revox B215's four Dolby B/C ICs).
standout_why: Rival pages compared: StereoNET (cited in all 3 chats) lists the W-1200 only as 'noise reduction' with no Dolby type and does not separate encode from decode for any deck. It never mentions the Tascam. Tape Lab (cited) gives no technical specs for the W-1200 or 202MKVII: no tape types, no NR, no head count. Home Audio Advice (2026-11-01, rank 4) says the W-1200 'includes Dolby B noise reduction', which suggests it records with Dolby B. It doesn't mention metal-tape recording or head layout. Portcycling and Headphonesty returned 403, so I could not compare them. Our own current page already says 'playback only' in the NR cell, but it does not explain the 2-head / single-NR-circuit reason or the metal-tape limit, and it does not tie either to the vintage-versus-new split.
decides: This confirms the split ChatGPT only hinted at ('not as high-fidelity'), and it gives the physical reason. For playing and digitizing existing tapes, the W-1200 or 202MKVII works: Dolby B-equivalent decode on playback, USB at up to 48 kHz/16-bit, Type I/II/IV playback. For making new recordings at the best quality, the new decks can't do it. They record un-encoded on Type I/II only, with no off-tape monitoring. A shopper who wants to record needs a serviced 3-head deck with record-side Dolby: Nakamichi CR-7A or Dragon, Revox B215, Sony TC-KA7ES (Dolby S). Pick the W-1200 for a buy-new playback and ripping deck. Pick the CR-7A or B215 for recording.

findings.label: Noise reduction is playback-only
findings.value: NR 'only functions during playback'; 'This cannot be used when recording to achieve a noise reduction effect like Dolby B.'
findings.source_title: Teac W-1200 Double Cassette Deck Owner's Manual (ManualsLib copy of TEAC manual)
findings.note: TEAC's own owner's manual text, read on the ManualsLib mirror. The TEAC US product URL (teac.com/us/product/w-1200/spec) redirected to a dead datarecorder.teac.com page.

findings.label: Recordable tape types
findings.value: Records Type I and Type II only; plays Type I, II and IV. 'This unit does not support recording to metal (type IV) tapes'
findings.source_title: Teac W-1200 Double Cassette Deck Owner's Manual (ManualsLib copy of TEAC manual)

findings.label: Head layout
findings.value: 1 recording/playback head + 1 erase head per deck (2-head, no separate playback head, so no off-tape monitoring)
findings.source_title: Teac W-1200 Double Cassette Deck Owner's Manual (ManualsLib copy of TEAC manual)
findings.note: Manual: 'Recording/playback head (1 each for TAPE 1 and TAPE 2)', 'Erase head (1 each for TAPE 1 and TAPE 2)'. The no-off-tape-monitoring point follows from having one combined head; the manual does not say it in those words.

findings.label: USB audio output
findings.value: USB 2.0 Full Speed, 8–48 kHz, 8/16-bit, standard OS driver (no install)
findings.source_title: Teac W-1200 Double Cassette Deck Owner's Manual (ManualsLib copy of TEAC manual)
findings.note: The manual's computer setup example suggests '2 channel, 16 bit, 48000 Hz'.

findings.label: Noise reduction is playback-only
findings.value: 'Noise reduction function to reduce hiss during playback (equivalent to Dolby B NR)'
findings.note: Maker's US page. It calls the NR 'equivalent to' Dolby B, not Dolby B, and describes it for playback only.

findings.label: Recordable tape types
findings.value: Records and plays Type I and Type II; 'For metal tapes (Type IV), only playback is supported.'

findings.label: Heads, response, flutter, USB
findings.value: Record/playback head ×1 + erase head ×1 per deck; 30 Hz–15 kHz ±4 dB (Type II), 30 Hz–13 kHz ±4 dB (Type I); wow and flutter 0.25% W.RMS; USB-B, up to 48 kHz/16-bit; pitch ±12% on TAPE 1 only
findings.note: Maker's US spec page. The 202MKVII and W-1200 share the same head layout and NR approach.

findings.label: Heads and record-side Dolby
findings.value: 3 discrete heads with off-tape monitoring; Dolby B and C with 'Double Dolby NR Circuits'; the 3-head design 'requires a Double Dolby system, one for recording and one for playback'
findings.note: Enthusiast reference site that reproduces Nakamichi feature text. Sold 1982–1993. Records normal, chrome and metal tapes.

findings.label: NAAC auto-azimuth scope
findings.value: 'Auto Playback Azimuth Correction': adjusts the azimuth of the playback head
findings.note: Described as a playback feature. It is the reason the Dragon plays other decks' tapes well, which is the playback case ChatGPT praised it for.

findings.label: Heads, NR, calibration
findings.value: 3 discrete heads, off-tape monitoring; Dolby B and C (Dolby C 'provides 20 dB of noise reduction above about 1,000 Hz'); manual playback azimuth; auto bias and auto level calibration; normal/chrome/metal

findings.label: Record-side Dolby and auto calibration
findings.value: Four Hitachi Dolby B/C ICs in a 'double Dolby' configuration (independent encode and decode); auto calibration adjusts bias and sensitivity separately per channel, 8 measurements per adjustment by binary search; four-motor direct-drive transport
findings.note: Encyclopedia summary, not the maker. Built 1985 to about 1990.

findings.label: Heads, NR, calibration
findings.value: 3 heads (erase 1, record 1, play 1); Dolby S NR and Dolby HX-PRO; 3-point record calibration (400 Hz, 3 kHz, 15 kHz); 15 Hz–22 kHz ±3 dB at −20 dB (metal, EIAJ); released 1995 at ¥120,000
findings.note: Japanese spec database. The page does not list Dolby B/C.

findings.label: Rival page wording on W-1200 NR
findings.value: Home Audio Advice says the W-1200 'includes Dolby B noise reduction, so tapes recorded with Dolby B play back as intended'; StereoNET lists only 'noise reduction'
findings.source_title: Best Cassette Players 2026: Tape Decks and Portables (Home Audio Advice)
findings.note: Neither page says the NR does nothing when recording. StereoNET was read at https://www.stereonet.com/buyers-guides/best-cassette-players-2026 on 2026-11-08.

unsourced: TEAC's own US spec page for the W-1200: teac.com/us/product/w-1200/spec 301-redirects to a 404 on datarecorder.teac.com, and the teac.jp/int spec and feature pages render through script and returned no spec text. The manual text came from the ManualsLib mirror instead.

Whether Dolby has stopped licensing or making B/C/S NR ICs, which would explain why new decks are 'equivalent to Dolby B' and decode only. The TechHive 202MKVII review that reportedly says this returned HTTP 410, and a search found no Dolby or maker statement.
Whether the W-1200 or 202MKVII decodes Dolby C or Dolby S tapes. Maker pages name only a Dolby B equivalent, and I found no explicit statement that C/S tapes are unsupported.
Sony TC-KA7ES Dolby B/C support: audio-database lists only Dolby S and HX-PRO, and I did not open a second source.
Whether the Nakamichi Dragon's NAAC also works while recording: naks.com describes it only as playback azimuth correction.
TEAC AD-850-SE head layout and NR behavior (not checked).
